en: Ritual for Paying Homage to the Buddha (to be performed six times daily and nightly, or three times a day, or twice at dawn and dusk).
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Hongzan of Baoliang Forest Monastery in Nanhai, Guangzhou.

(In the present day, many acts of prostration deviate from the ritual rules and fail to accord with the teachings. Some call out names out of order and remain ignorant of extolling and praising the Buddha’s supreme virtues; others lack reverence and do not know how to repent, make vows, and dedicate the merit.)

If one does not understand the Dharma, by what means could one cast off the dust of worldly defilements to obtain merit and thereby summon the ultimate fruit? Therefore, both the sutras and the śāstras present five dharmas, among which they highly esteem reverent salutation and the praise of virtue. First, one must proceed to the incense altar, straighten the body, and quiet the mind.
One should contemplate the holy virtues while beholding the venerable countenance. With both knees touching the ground and hands holding an incense burner, one recites these verses:

The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, and the fragrance of liberation—clouds of radiant light pervading the entire Dharma-realm—make offerings to the infinite Buddhas of the ten directions;

by smelling these fragrances, all are universally perfumed and realize nirvana. (This verse is from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. It refers to the fragrance of the fivefold Dharma-body; for the sake of composing this verse, the text is abbreviated, omitting the fragrance of wisdom and the fragrance of the knowledge and vision of liberation.)

Incense: Since incense acts as the messenger of the Buddha, it is offered first. Alternatively, one may use the verse for the clouds of ordinary incense and flowers, with this modification: "And to all the Pratyekabuddhas and Rishis. If there are fresh flowers, they should be used and held aloft for offering.

○ Universal Prostration to the Triple Gem (First, one should praise their virtues. Whichever Buddha, Bodhisattva, or Noble Sangha one prostrates to, one should praise them according to their virtues. As for the words of praise, one may take verses from various sutras and śāstras.)

These serve as expressions of deep sighs. If one’s words of praise do not accord with the person’s actual virtues, one may instead compose verses of praise based on the intent of the scriptures. Herein, I have briefly extracted one hundred verses compiled by the worthy and holy to praise the Triple Gem.

Furthermore, whenever performing prostrations, one must first revere the Triple Gem. The Triple Gem is the most supreme auspiciousness, a field of merit that provides excellent blessings; it can eliminate the karmic defilements of sentient beings, repel all demonic obstacles, and ensure that all virtuous deeds performed attain fulfillment.
(The Praise to the Buddha follows:)
I prostrate to all those who have transcended the world, the most honored in the three realms, oceans of merit. You, the wise ones, can incinerate the defilements of affliction;

O Perfectly Awakened Ones, I now take refuge and pay homage to you. (If one can recite the mantra for extinguishing sins before performing this prostration, it is most excellent. The mantra is as follows:)
Namo daśana (1) | Buddha-koṭi-na (2) | Oṃ (3) | Huru huru (4) | Siddha-rocani (5) | Sarva-ratha (6) | Sthāni (7) | Svāhā. (The *Ratnaketu-dhāraṇī-sūtra* states:
This mantra was spoken by ten koṭis of Buddhas. I now likewise, out of compassion for all sentient beings, [speak it]. For those who uphold this mantra, it can cause all...)

All sentient beings who harbor anger and malice shall become entirely joyful. If one can recite this mantra and perform prostrations three times each day, it surpasses the merit of prostrating before a thousand million *koṭi* of Buddhas. After the end of one’s life, one will attain rebirth in the Western Land of the Buddha Amitāyus.

Furthermore, it is said that at the time of death, one will be welcomed by all the Buddhas, and in the future *Bhadrakalpa*, one will personally receive and make offerings to each of the thousand Buddhas. Indeed, for anyone who can constantly recite this mantra, the merit is most inconceivable.

With single-minded devotion, prostrate to all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions and the three periods of time. (One must perform a full prostration with the five limbs touching the ground, hands reaching toward the sky to manifest the gesture of receiving the Buddhas’ feet.

Then, one should cultivate this visualization: "The nature of the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and tranquil; the resonance between cause and response is inconceivable. My place of practice is like the jewels of Indra’s net, wherein the reflections of the Buddhas of the ten directions appear.

My own reflection appears before all the Buddhas; with head meeting their feet, I take refuge and pay homage. If prostrating to the Original Teacher, one should say: "Within the reflection of Śākyamuni Tathāgata... When paying homage to other Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Holy Sangha, adapt the text accordingly as above. (To praise the Dharma, say:)

I prostrate to the one who can pull us from the perils of birth and death, who universally dries up the ocean of sorrow, affliction, greed, and delusion, and who shatters the mountains of worldly toil and sinful karma;
I now take refuge and pay homage to the Jewel of the Sublime Dharma.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to all Honored Dharmas of the ten directions and the three periods of time. (Recite: "The Dharma-nature of true emptiness is like space; the eternally abiding Dharma Jewel is inconceivable."
My form appears before the Jewel of the Dharma; with single-minded devotion, I take refuge and pay homage according to the Dharma. (Praise the Saṅgha:

I bow my head in reverence to all Buddhas who are praised, whose adornments are the myriad practices of the Eightfold Path, and whose unconditioned concentration and wisdom gradually become perfect and luminous.
I now take refuge in the Jewel of the Noble Assembly.

With single-minded devotion, prostrate to all the worthy and holy Sanghas of the ten directions and the three periods of time (visualize as before; this praise and prostration includes both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna Sanghas).

○ Prostrate to Śākyamuni Bhagavān (the hymn may be either the verse "In heaven above and on earth below, there is none like the Buddha," or the "Praise of the Tathāgata’s Sublime Form Body"; either is acceptable. This is the manner of reverent salutation in the Western Regions).

They were extensively arranged as hymns of praise, such as those composed by the Venerable Mātṛceṭa, who, following the Buddha’s prior prophecy, created four hundred verses and one hundred and fifty stanzas. These collectively expound the six perfections and clarify the Buddha’s supreme virtues; their phrasing is elegant and beautiful, while their principles are pure and sublime.

Great masters such as Asaṅga, Vasubandhu, and Aśvaghoṣa all took them as their ancestral models. Beginners must not fail to know them. The Tathāgata’s golden body is sixteen feet tall, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs, and his bodily radiance extends one fathom.
The white tuft of hair between his brows shines universally throughout the ten directions, as described in the Vaipulya Sūtras. As the Bodhisattva Puṣpaketu praises the Buddha in verse:
"The physical body of the World-Honored One is like a mountain of gold, Like a thousand suns illuminating the world. He is able to uproot all suffering and affliction;
I now prostrate before the Great Dharma King."
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to our original teacher, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni.

Prostrate to Amitābha Buddha (in the language of China, *Wúliàngshòu Fó*; as stated in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*: "The body of Amitābha Buddha is sixty million *koṭi-nayuta* Ganges-sand *yojana*s in height").

The eyes are like the waters of the four great oceans; the white tuft of hair between the brows is like the five Mount Sumerus; and the radiance of the body is like a hundred billion triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems. Yet this is not something that can be reached by the mental power of ordinary beings.

By the power of the Buddha, one will surely achieve accomplishment through recollection. Merely visualizing the Buddha’s image yields immeasurable merit; how much more so if one can contemplate the Buddha’s complete physical marks, or even perform the visualization of the sixteen-foot body. (This too is achieved.)
Adorned by a multitude of virtues beyond measure, his radiance shines universally throughout the ten directions. Among the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, none can equal him;
he constantly extends the great vessel of compassion to all sentient beings.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the World-Honored One Amitābha of the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Next, prostrate to Maitreya Bodhisattva. (According to the *Sūtra on the Descent* regarding his descent when the human lifespan reaches eighty thousand years, the Buddha’s body will be thirty-two *zhang* tall.

However, according to his present form in Tuṣita Heaven, the Great Being’s physical stature is sixteen *yojanas*. His marks and signs are like those of a Buddha. Upon his celestial jewel crown are manifested countless transformation Buddhas, transformation Bodhisattvas, and great Bodhisattvas from other directions.)

Dwelling within his celestial crown, if one recites the name of Maitreya for even a single moment, the transgressions of birth and death accumulated over twelve hundred kalpas will be eliminated. Merely hearing his name and joining one's palms in reverent homage eliminates the transgressions of birth and death accumulated over five thousand kalpas.

If one pays full prostration and reverence, the transgressions of birth and death accumulated over ten billion kalpas will be eliminated, as stated in the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above*. Thus it is praised.

The Great Being attained Equal and Perfect Enlightenment long ago; to mature sentient beings, he dwells in Tuṣita. Day and night he constantly turns the irreversible wheel, delivering beings through the three assemblies under the Dragon-Flower tree—his merit is infinite.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the World-Honored One Maitreya, who will descend to be born in the future.

Prostrate to Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva. (This Bodhisattva possesses great wisdom and eloquence; he is the Son of the Dharma King and the Teacher of all Buddhas. He manifests in the form of a youth with five topknots on his head and a purple body, wearing precious necklaces and seated upon a precious lotus flower.

As for the description of him "sitting upon a lion," it symbolizes that when the Bodhisattva preaches the Dharma, it is like the roar of a lion, causing all beasts to hide their tracks. Within Jambudvīpa, all sentient beings receive the benefit of this Bodhisattva’s virtue.)

This protection must be known. If one recites this name even once, immeasurable sins will be extinguished and immeasurable merit will increase; one shall attain Buddhahood in the future, titled the Tathāgata Universal Manifestation (Puxian). As it is praised: (End of quote)

The Teacher of the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time, whose wisdom and vows are vast and inconceivable; he shall universally manifest as the Sugata in the future, taking the boundless oceans of lands as his realm.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī of Great Wisdom.

Prostrate to Samantabhadra Bodhisattva (who possesses great conduct and vows; is the eldest son of all Buddhas; wears a flower crown upon his head and is draped in jeweled necklaces; sits upon a precious lotus flower, or rides a six-tusked white elephant to symbolize the six perfections and myriad practices).

If one takes refuge in Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, then all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions will provide their protection. This is because all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have attained their state by practicing the three mysteries and performing the conduct of Samantabhadra.
This is because he has realized the fruits of the noble path. It is praised thus:

A six-tusked white elephant serves as his jeweled throne; The myriad practices of the perfections constitute his gestures and expressions. In the Flower Treasury World, he is hailed as the eldest son;
Throughout the lands of the ten directions, he manifests his entire body.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra of Great Conduct.

I pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. (This Bodhisattva attained Buddhahood in the past, being named Tathāgata Saddharmaprabhāsa. He now currently serves as the Bodhisattva of the Position of Succession in the Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*).

In the future, he shall succeed Amitābha Buddha upon his seat and attain Buddhahood, being named Tathāgata Samantaprabhā-ucca-vyūha-śrī-kūṭarāja. However, because he has a karmic affinity with the sentient beings of this world, he manifests thirty-two forms of response to teach and transform them. Fundamentally...)

His body was the color of purple-gold. He was eighty million *nayuta* yojanas tall. On his head was a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*), and around his neck was a halo. Within this light were five hundred transformation Buddhas and five hundred bodhisattvas.

Within the light of his entire body, the various forms and appearances of all sentient beings in the five realms of existence were manifested. Upon his head, within a precious celestial crown, stood a transformation Buddha twenty-five yojanas high.

The tuft of hair between his eyebrows was the color of the seven jewels, emitting eighty-four thousand rays of light. His arms were the color of red lotuses, adorned with eighteen billion exquisite lights as necklaces. His palms were the color of five hundred billion variegated lotuses, and on the tips of his ten fingers were eighty-four thousand painted patterns, radiant and soft.

It universally illumines all. With this jewel-hand, he receives and guides sentient beings. For such a bodhisattva, merely hearing his name brings immeasurable merit. The rest is as explained in the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Alternatively, for those who are unable to perform this visualization, it may be done according to the capacity of one's mind.
It is also so. Regarding *nayuta*: ten billion (*wan-qi*) makes one *nayuta*. Forty *li* makes one *yojana*. Ten billion makes one *koṭi*. Thus it is praised.

The Buddha atop the jeweled crown embodies cause within effect; the Dharma-Heavenly Teacher of the past, through the movement of his compassionate vows, manifests a thousand hands and eyes to care for all sentient beings without missing the proper time.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, Greatly Compassionate and Greatly Merciful.

[Prostrate] to the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta. (This Bodhisattva’s physical stature is equal to that of Avalokiteśvara. The radiance of his entire body illuminates the lands of the ten directions; all sentient beings with whom he has a karmic connection are able to see him.

With the light of wisdom, he universally illumines all, causing them to leave the sufferings of the three miserable realms and attain immeasurable power; therefore, he is named Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Within his celestial crown are five hundred jeweled flowers, and each flower has five hundred jeweled pedestals. Each...

The pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions appear within this [image]. Upon the *uṣṇīṣa* is a jeweled vase containing various radiances that universally manifest Buddha-activities. The rest is as described in the sutra. (Praise: The pure lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions All appear therein. Upon the *uṣṇīṣa* is a single jeweled vase, Filling it with all manner of radiances, Universally manifesting the deeds of the Buddhas. The remainder is as explained in the sutra. (Praise:)
The jeweled vase upon his crown manifests the Buddha’s deeds; within a single pore, he perceives the ten directions. Raising his foot, he causes all lands to tremble;
he universally gathers pure beings to return to the Land of Bliss.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Next, prostrate to the Bodhisattva Kṣitigarbha. This Bodhisattva’s physical form is upright and majestic, and his awesome virtue is preeminent; with the sole exception of the Tathāgata, none among Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, or others can surpass him.

Furthermore, regarding all the teachings and transformations within this world-system, with the sole exception of Samantabhadra, Avalokiteśvara, and other great Bodhisattvas, none can equal him. Having long ago attained the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), his merits are fully perfected, and he manifests throughout the ten directions by the power of his original vows.

In this world of five turbidities, his transformative benefits are especially profound. He swiftly fulfills all that sentient beings seek, extinguishes all grave offenses, removes all obstacles, and brings about immediate peace and security. If one performs even a single prostration or a single offering, immeasurable sins will be extinguished.
One obtains immeasurable merit. (The praise says:
"Your compassionate vow first arose from the rescue of your kin; how could one measure your emanated bodies as they universally deliver all? You shall not attain Buddhahood until hell is emptied.
I now prostrate before the King of Great Vows."
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Kṣitigarbha.
Prostrate to the Bodhisattva Gaganagañja. (This Bodhisattva wears necklaces and ornaments; within the flower crown upon his head is a blue maṇi jewel.

If one contemplates this jewel, immeasurable sins are extinguished and immeasurable obstacles are removed. Therefore, in the practice of repentance, this Bodhisattva is taken as the presiding lord for the extinction of sin. For those who seek discernment and wisdom, it is as stated in the *Gaganagañja Sūtra*. The praise says:)
The blue light of the jewel upon his crown shines brilliantly; he extinguishes the sins of sentient beings as if they were empty space. I now prostrate and repent before the Lord of Confession;
the three obstacles are instantly eliminated, and merit and wisdom are harmoniously integrated.
With single-minded devotion, I prostrate to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Ākāśagarbha.

I pay homage to the Venerable Kāśyapa (the Treasury of the Śāstras of Dharani; skilled in instruction and guidance; entrusted with the grand governing principles; who practiced the twelve dhūtas; whose bodily form was golden in color;
whom the Tathāgata charged with the Eye-Treasury of the True Dharma). Praise says:
His virtuous marks are as majestic and upright as a mass of gold; he has practiced the ascetic dhūta austerities throughout his entire life.
Having personally inherited the Tathāgata’s True Dharma Eye, he awaits the Compassionate Honored One within Mount Kukkuṭapāda.
With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.

Prostrate to the Venerable Upāli (who led the fourfold assembly, was skilled in understanding the Vinaya Piṭaka, and was foremost in upholding the discipline; as he was the senior elder of the Venerable Ānanda, he is honored first, and is praised as follows).
He attained liberation before the eight princes; at the assembly of the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, he realized perfect penetration.
He propagated the Vinaya teachings of the Piṇī-piṭaka, whereby the Buddha-dharma flourished and remained in the world.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Venerable Upāli;

I pay homage to the Venerable Ānanda (the upholder of the Piṭaka of Sūtras, who personally attended the Tathāgata, was foremost in erudition, was the Tathāgata’s cousin, and possessed thirty of the marks of a Great Man). I praise him thus:
Renowned as the foremost among those of great learning, having realized the Way, his body transcended the four modes of deportment.
He compiled the Tathāgata’s treasury of the True Dharma, forever serving as a teacher who delivers beings in the realms of humans and devas.

With single-minded devotion, prostrate to the Venerable Ānanda (as above, offering one prostration for each; three prostrations are even better). If you further prostrate to other Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, whether ten times or a hundred times, do so according to your own inclination.

○ The Fivefold Method of Repentance (1. Prostration; 2. Confession; 3. Rejoicing; 4. Entreaty; 5. Aspiration and Dedication). As stated in the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra*: The Buddha told Ānanda and Maitreya Bodhisattva:

“When I originally sought the Way, I did not attain the path of Buddhahood by offering my ears, nose, head, eyes, hands, feet, body, life, precious treasures, wife, children, or kingdom as alms. Rather, it was through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and the practice of peace and happiness that I attained the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

What are these skillful means? Day and night, at each of the three periods, one should adjust one’s robes and bind one’s body, kneel with the knees touching the ground, and address the Buddhas of the ten directions, saying:”
I repent of all my transgressions; I exhort and assist the multitude toward the Way and its virtue; I take refuge and pay homage to all Buddhas, so that they may attain unsurpassed wisdom.

[Note on the commentary: "Repenting" refers to the confession of all evil faults committed through body, speech, and mind since beginningless time. "Exhorting" refers to requesting all Bodhisattvas throughout the ten directions who have not yet attained Buddhahood to swiftly achieve it.

"Buddha" refers to those who have already attained Buddhahood; may they remain forever in the world, turning the wheel of the True Dharma and not entering *nirvāṇa*, so as to bring benefit and happiness to sentient beings.

"Assisting" means to rejoice in all the merits of both ordinary beings and sages; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, may one forever abandon thoughts of malice toward all living beings. Whatever merits they cultivate and study, even down to a single hair’s breadth of goodness, I now assist and rejoice in them all.

"Taking refuge" means to offer up one's own life to take refuge in all Buddhas; this is to prostrate with bodies as numerous as the atoms of all lands before Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of all lands. "Causing [them] to attain unsurpassed wisdom" means that by means of these four kinds of merit and all the good deeds thus cultivated, one vows to dedicate them all entirely.

I bestow [the merit] upon all sentient beings so that we may together realize the unsurpassed wisdom of the seed of perfect enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi). Generally speaking, all acts of repentance and the making of vows do not transcend these five dharmas. Although they are presented together in various sutras, those texts are extensive while this one is concise.

For those who prefer a detailed account, they should consult such works as the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* and the "Chapter on Vows" (*Pranidhāna-paṭala*). Next, one should pay homage to the Triple Gem on behalf of sovereigns, parents, and others.

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the assembly of celestial dragons and the eight classes of beings who protect the Dharma. I prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions.

(The prayer says: "I only pray that the celestial dragons and the eight classes of beings will increase their majestic radiance, protect the True Teaching, and ensure that the fourfold assembly remains peaceful and harmonious, free from all demonic obstacles."

With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to the Emperor, the high ministers, the officials, and the patrons who protect the Dharma. I prostrate before the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions.

(I pray that the imperial domain may remain firm and secure, the sovereign way may flourish far and wide, the ranks of civil and military officials may increase in merit, and the Triple Gem may prosper. May the four seasons be harmoniously regulated, the scholars and commoners find joy in their vocations, and the patrons enjoy overflowing blessings, never encountering the three calamities or the eight hardships.)
Until the attainment of unsurpassed Bodhi, I single-mindedly dedicate this to my parents.
I prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions, praying that my two parents may increase in merit, blessings, and longevity.

Their wisdom is perfectly clear and bright. If their parents of the past have transcended their spirits to the Pure Land and exhausted their karma in the realm of toil, they shall see the opening of flowers of the highest grade and receive the prediction of Buddhahood within one lifetime.
With single-minded devotion, I pay homage to my Upādhyāya and Ācārya, and to the Three Jewels eternally abiding throughout the ten directions.

(I pray that my Upādhyāya and Ācārya may have harmony in the four great elements, that their lifespan may equal the Dharma-body, and that their merit and wisdom may increase and flourish, universally benefiting all beings. If they have passed away, one should say: "May their rank and status be further exalted.")

With single-minded devotion, on behalf of the disciples of the fourfold assembly in the Dharma-ending age, I prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions (may the roots of goodness of the fourfold assembly be forever firm;
may they advance upon the Path without demonic interference, and swiftly realize unsurpassed Bodhi).
With single-minded devotion, on behalf of all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm, I prostrate to the eternally abiding Triple Gem of the ten directions.

(I pray that all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm may simultaneously attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Herein, one may increase, decrease, or add further aspirations according to one's own intention; they are not elaborated upon here.)
○ Appendix: Verses from the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* (The Chapter on the Questions of Maitreya Bodhisattva) [Volume I].

(The verses for the five repentances are abbreviated here. Fearing that the sentiment of earnest supplication would not be fully expressed, yet that the text of other sūtras would be too extensive for beginners to recite, I have now appended the verses from the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra*. Their length is moderate, making them convenient for recitation.)

The Buddha told Ānanda: "In the past, when Maitreya was practicing the bodhisattva path, during the six periods of day and night, he bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in homage before the Buddhas, and recited these verses."
I now take refuge and pay homage to all the Buddhas of the ten directions, to the assembly of Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas, and to the Great Sages who possess the divine eye;

I also pay homage to the bodhicitta. It keeps one far removed from all evil realms, enables rebirth in the heavens, and leads even to the realization of Nirvāṇa. If I have committed even the slightest transgression—
In accordance with what arises in the mind, now before the presence of all Buddhas, I repent so that [faults] may be eliminated.
May the various merits accumulated by my body, speech, and mind now serve as the cause for Bodhi;
may I attain the Unsurpassed Way. Among the lands of the ten directions, those who make offerings to the Tathāgatas—
And the unsurpassed wisdom of the Buddhas— I now rejoice in it all. Whatever transgressions I have committed, I confess them all;
All this merit I rejoice in. I now pay homage to all the Buddhas; May I attain unsurpassed wisdom.
To the Great Bodhisattvas of the ten directions Who have realized the ten stages, I now prostrate with my head in reverence.
May you swiftly realize enlightenment; having realized enlightenment, may you subdue the armies of Māra and turn the wondrous, pure wheel of Dharma for the benefit of all classes of sentient beings.
May you always remain in the world for immeasurable koṭis of kalpas, beating the great drum of the Dharma to deliver suffering beings.
I am submerged in the mire of desire, bound by the ropes of craving, and entangled in manifold fetters;
may the Buddhas deign to observe me. Although sentient beings are heavily defiled, the Buddhas never weary of or abandon them;
may they, through great compassion, deliver us from the ocean of birth and death, O World-Honored Ones of the present.
The path of the bodhisattva traversed by the Buddhas of the past and future— may I now vow to practice and study it, fulfilling the pāramitās,
accomplishing the six supernormal powers, and delivering all sentient beings. May I realize the unsurpassed way,
thoroughly understanding that all phenomena are empty, signless, and devoid of intrinsic nature.
Non-abiding and non-indicative, neither arising nor ceasing; Furthermore, like the Great Sage who thoroughly understands selflessness, There is no *pudgala*, nor even a life-principle (*jīva*).
Regarding all matters of giving, he does not grasp at "I" or "mine," In order to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings.
Giving without stinginess, may the objects I give arise without effort;
through observing and realizing emptiness, I fulfill the perfection of generosity.
Maintaining discipline without deficiency, I attain the pure śīla of a Buddha; because of non-abiding, I fulfill the perfection of ethical conduct.
Enduring patience is like the four great elements, Giving rise to no discriminating mind;

Because of being free from anger, one fulfills the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*). By the power of body and mind, I vow to initiate great diligence, firm and without indolence, Fulfilling the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*), Through that which is like an illusion or a magical transformation.
And with courageous diligence, through vajra-like samādhis, and endowed with the perfection of dhyāna,
may you realize the wisdom of samādhi; entering the three gates of liberation, realizing the equality of the three times, and endowed with the perfection of prajñā—
may you attain the wondrous form-body of all Buddhas, its radiance and great majestic power.
"May I fulfill all the practices of the bodhisattva’s diligent application.
Maitreya, the one of renowned fame, diligently cultivates such practices, being endowed with the six pāramitās and dwelling securely in the ten stages.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "The Bodhisattva Maitreya dwells in such skillful means and accumulates the unsurpassed [merit]."
Bodhi. Ānanda, in the past when I sought the Way, I underwent immeasurable suffering before being able to accumulate unsurpassed Bodhi.

(The twenty-four verses above: the first two are verses of homage; the third is a verse of repentance; the fourth is a verse of making vows; the fifth is a verse of sympathetic joy; the sixth is a verse on dedicating the merit of repentance, sympathetic joy, and prostrations to the Buddha toward the unsurpassed Way;

the seventh and eighth are verses requesting the turning of the Wheel of Dharma; the ninth is a verse requesting the Buddha to remain in the world; the tenth and eleventh are verses seeking the Buddha’s acceptance, which also correspond to the first two of the Four Great Vows; the twelfth is a verse on following the Buddha in study.)

Phonetic Glossary.
Dakṣa (also written as Taśa) na-ūṃ (the two syllables combined to form the sound Oṃ) sarva (alternatively *sa*-*ba*, with the *ba* pronounced in the departing tone).
The *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha-sūtra* states: "Recite this three times."
Prostrate once. To prostrate in this manner three times eradicates all ten evil deeds, the five heinous crimes, the four grave offenses, and other such transgressions;
all obstacles and difficulties are completely extinguished. This merit is equal to that of a superior person prostrating before ten trillion Buddhas.
This is called the *namo-sigara* mantra; in the language of China, it is called the "Mantra of Prostration."

*Duṭo* (dhūta) is also called *duda*; in the language of China, it means "to shake off. This refers to practicing twelve ascetic practices, which serve to shake off the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the three realms.
Regarding the three calamities and the three great calamities: fire, water, and wind cause the destruction of the world. The three minor calamities are weapons, famine, and [pestilence].
Famine; pestilence; and the eight difficulties:
first, the hells; second, the animal realm; third, the hungry ghosts; fourth, the heaven of non-conception, wherein one cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma;
fifth, the continent of Uttarakuru, wherein one cannot see the Buddha or hear the Dharma; sixth, being blind, deaf, or mute; seventh...
"Worldly wisdom and eloquence" refers to the sharp and clever worldly intelligence that indulges in non-Buddhist texts and does not believe in the supramundane True Dharma.
"Eight births before or after a Buddha" means that due to heavy karma and thin roots of merit, one does not encounter a Buddha’s appearance in the world or hear the Buddha preach the Dharma.
The Great Sage Buddha is the Sage among Sages, the God among Gods, and the Immortal among Immortals; thus he is called the Great Awakened Golden Immortal (*Mahābuddha-suvarṇakṣānti*).

*Nirvāṇa* is the Chinese translation for "Perfect Quiescence" (*yuánjì*). This means that because his virtues are complete without exception, it is called "perfect" (*yuán*); because his obstructions are exhausted without exception, it is called "quiescent" (*jì*).
The former [translation] says "neither arising nor ceasing.
*Pudgala*—in the language of China, "one who repeatedly takes up [existence]" (*shuququ*)—is an alternative designation for a sentient being (*sattva*).
This refers to how all living beings repeatedly go and come, moving toward rebirth within the six realms of existence.
The six destinies (*ṣaḍ-gati*) are the six realms: first, the gods; second, humans; third, asuras; fourth, hell-beings; fifth, hungry ghosts; and sixth, animals.
*Pāramitā* translates into Chinese as "reaching the other shore. This means that by practicing these six dharmas, one delivers oneself and others, reaching *nirvāṇa*.
Because it leads to the shore of liberation, it is also called the "Six Perfections" (ṣaṭpāramitā).
*Śīla* translates into Chinese as "coolness" (*qīngliáng*). This means that by upholding the precepts, one can eliminate afflictions and thereby attain coolness.

Samādhi is translated in the vernacular as "right concentration" (zhèngdìng). There are hundreds of thousands of samādhis; reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), one enters the Vajra Samādhi, severs the final subtle ignorance, and only then realizes the Buddha-ground.
The three gates of liberation are the three doors of deliverance: first, emptiness; second, signlessness; and third, wishlessness.
